After the inside becomes positive to about $+40 \text{ mV}$, the membrane must be reset. What must happen to the first type of channel and what second type must open?

walkthrough:
Setting Up Depolarisation**
At rest the inside is negative relative to the outside. When stimulated, voltage-gated Na+ channels in the axon membrane open. Na+ are at higher concentration outside, so they diffuse rapidly into the neurone down their electrochemical gradient. The influx of positive ions makes the inside positive, up to about $+40 \text{ mV}$. This reversal is depolarisation and forms the rising phase of the action potential.

Resetting With Repolarisation**
At the peak, Na+ channels close and voltage-gated K+ channels open. K+ are more concentrated inside, so they diffuse out of the cell. Loss of positive ions makes the inside negative again. This is repolarisation, restoring the resting potential. The sodium-potassium pump later restores the original ion gradients.

Why Myelin Changes The Pathway**
In a myelinated neurone, Schwann cells wrap the axon in fatty myelin. Myelin is an electrical insulator, it prevents ion movement across the membrane and so no action potential can form there. Gaps called nodes of Ranvier have exposed membrane with high density of Na+ and K+ channels. So depolarisation and action potentials occur only at nodes.

Saltatory Conduction Is Fast And One-Way**
Na+ entering at one node creates local circuits - local currents of positive charge that spread sideways inside the axon to the next node, bringing it to threshold and triggering a new action potential there. The impulse appears to jump from node to node. This is saltatory conduction. It is much faster because fewer action potentials are needed, and it is one-way because the previous node is in refractory period and cannot be re-stimulated immediately.

Final answer: Voltage-gated Na+ channels open, Na+ enter axon by diffusion, membrane depolarises to about $+40 \text{ mV}$. Then Na+ channels close and voltage-gated K+ channels open, K+ leave axon, membrane repolarises to negative. Local circuits spread depolarisation. Myelin sheath insulates axon and prevents ion movement, so action potentials occur only at nodes of Ranvier. This gives saltatory conduction, fast one-way transmission.

walkthrough:
Defining Homeostasis**
Homeostasis means keeping the internal environment stable despite external change. That includes blood, tissue fluid and cell conditions. Control is not perfectly fixed but held within narrow limits around a set point or optimum value by negative feedback. This provides stable conditions for cells.

Why Body Temperature Must Be Stable**
Mammalian enzymes work best around $37^{\circ}\text{C}$. If temperature is too low, molecules have less kinetic energy, fewer enzyme-substrate collisions occur, so metabolic and respiration rates fall. If temperature is too high, hydrogen bonds break, enzymes denature, lose their active site shape and cells are damaged. Both extremes can be fatal.

Why Blood Glucose Must Be Stable**
Glucose is the respiratory substrate for ATP production, and brain cells depend almost entirely on continuous glucose supply. Low blood glucose means cells cannot make enough ATP, leading to weakness, confusion, coma and death. High blood glucose lowers the water potential of blood, causes water loss from tissues by osmosis, increases blood volume and pressure, and long term damages kidneys, retina and blood vessels.

Why Blood Water Potential Must Be Stable**
Water potential affects osmosis between blood, tissue fluid and cells. If blood water potential is too low (too little water), water leaves cells by osmosis, cells crenate and blood pressure rises. If blood water potential is too high (too much water), water enters cells by osmosis, cells may swell and lyse, and blood pressure falls. Stable water potential protects cell volume and blood pressure.

Final answer: Homeostasis is maintenance of a constant internal environment within narrow limits around a set point / optimum. Low temperature slows enzyme activity and respiration; high temperature denatures enzymes and damages cells. Low blood glucose gives insufficient substrate for respiration, causing brain malfunction / coma; high blood glucose lowers blood water potential causing dehydration of tissues and organ damage. Low blood water potential draws water out of cells by osmosis; high blood water potential causes water uptake, cell lysis and low blood pressure.
